1) Setup and interpretation
- Let L(−) = Λ(−) = Map(S^1, −) be the free loop space functor. For a map f: X → Y, it induces f̃: LX → LY by precomposition. To form a fibration to analyze, compose LX with the evaluation map at a fixed basepoint y0 ∈ Y to obtain ev_y0 ∘ f̃: LX → {y0} ⊂ Y; this factors through the component of constant loops L_y0Y ⊂ LY. Equivalently, one works fiberwise over a chosen path from y0 to f(x0) to move basepoints and compare to the standard evaluation fibration. <cite id="c276e040-1">For a homotopy fibration f: X → Y, the pullback of the path-space fibration defines a model for the homotopy fiber, and these constructions extend to free loops via the fibration sequence associated to ev: ΛX → X</cite>. <cite id="e3c61afd-4">The evaluation map admits a pointed section when restricted to constant maps, making all π_n(ev) surjective and the connecting homomorphisms in the homotopy long exact sequence null; however, this splitting only exists into the component of the zero map, so analogous splittings fail for noncanonical basepoints</cite>.

2) General model: evaluation fibration and homotopy fiber
- The classical device is the path-space fibration PY → Y with fiber ΩY, and the homotopy pullback of f: X → Y along Y gives a homotopy fiber model F → X → Y. For free loops, one uses the analogous fibration sequence for evaluation ev: LX → X by constructing a homotopy pullback of the path-space fibration along f, which yields a model for the homotopy fiber of f̃: LX → LY over the constant loop on y0. <cite id="c276e040-1">Using the path-space fibration P Y → Y and its pullback along f, one obtains a homotopy equivalence between the homotopy fiber and the space obtained by pulling back the path fibration; this yields a fibration sequence extending the homotopy fibration F → X → Y to the level of free loops</cite>. <cite id="c276e040-4">For fibrations with path-connected base, any two fibers have the same homotopy type; h-fibrations are fiber homotopy equivalent to honest fibrations, providing tools to compare fibers of f̃ over different basepoints</cite>.

3) When the basepoint is a non-constant loop: relative loop space viewpoint and identifications
- To analyze the homotopy fiber of LX → LY over a non-constant loop β ∈ LY, it is useful to “promote” β to a basepoint in the total space by choosing a path γ: I → Y from y0 to β(1) such that γ(1) = β(1) and γ(0) = y0; then β is the composite ev_γ of the loop γ(1) = β(1) with a based loop at γ(1). The fiber over β can then be identified with the space of loops in X whose evaluation path in Y is homotopic to γ over the loop β (i.e., a homotopy from ev(α) to β). This fits into a relative loop space construction: fix a path γ in Y from y0 to β(1); define a “relative free loop space” ΛX/γ as the space of loops α in X together with a homotopy from ev(α) to β, and then take the fiber of LX → LY over β. <cite id="c276e040-1">The free loop evaluation fibration and its pullbacks provide the template to replace Y by a model over the basepoint component via the path fibration</cite>. <cite id="e3c61afd-2">In explicit computations, the basepoint for a homotopy fiber of a fibration F → E → B over a nontrivial point may not be a constant map; instead it can be a map constant on components (e.g., a basepoint in a fiber over a non-constant loop), and the fiber can be modeled as the space of sections extending such a basepoint</cite>. <cite id="e3c61afd-1">Iterated and stabilized versions of these fibers (e.g., after applying Ω or Q) can be identified via basepoint-twisted mapping spaces; the basepoint is then a non-constant loop in the mapping target rather than a constant map</cite>.

4) Consequences: exact sequences and basepoint-dependent splittings
- In the based-loop setting, taking the free loop based at a point x0 ∈ X and mapping to the free loop based at f(x0) ∈ Y yields an exact sequence that connects π1(LX, x0) and π1(LY, f(x0)). In particular, when the homotopy class of f is fixed, the fundamental group of the fiber (over the corresponding component) identifies with the kernel of the induced map on based loops; this gives an algebraic model for the homotopy fiber. <cite id="e3c61afd-3">For the fibration ΩM → P M → BM (with evaluation at the basepoint), there is a long exact sequence of homotopy groups; there are isomorphisms π1(L(M), f_b) ≅ π1(LM, f_β), where f_b is a representative based loop and f_β its free homotopy class</cite>. <cite id="e3c61afd-4">The evaluation map of free loops has a splitting into the component of the zero map, hence all π_n(ev) are surjective and the connecting homomorphisms in the LES vanish on that component; yet the analogous splitting fails when one uses a noncanonical basepoint, reflecting that the fiber over a non-constant loop does not admit a universal section</cite>.
